summary: The bill authorizes $190 million for CDC and NIH programs to expand data collection, surveillance, and research on maternal health outcomes during public health emergencies, requires public release of disaggregated data on infections and outcomes among pregnant and postpartum people, directs education campaigns, and creates a task force to recommend policies for respectful maternity care.

scores.thoughts: The bill explicitly authorizes $190 million in new appropriations ($100M for CDC surveillance, $30M for ERASE MM, $45M for PRAMS, $15M for NICHD research) to expand federal data collection, surveillance, and research programs on maternal health during public health emergencies. This directly increases federal outlays.
The bill contains no provisions related to tax rates, credits, deductions, or revenue measures.

The legislation focuses on federal public-health surveillance, data transparency, CDC/CMS programs, Medicaid reimbursement references, and recommendations for respectful maternity care. It strengthens the public-sector role in maternal-health monitoring and guidance rather than promoting private-market mechanisms.
No references to firearms, gun regulations, or Second Amendment issues appear in the text.
Section 5(b)(1)(P) directs the task force to address needs of undocumented pregnant individuals, implying expanded consideration and protections for this population during emergencies.
The bill does not address abortion access, restrictions, or related services.
No provisions concern military or defense spending.
The legislation contains no environmental or climate-related content.
The bill references Medicaid coverage for doulas and perinatal support services and targets underserved populations, modestly expanding the scope of public maternal-health safety-net activities.
No education-policy provisions are present.
The task force is instructed to address substance-use disorder screening and treatment in pregnancy and postpartum periods, favoring public-health treatment approaches over stricter enforcement.
No criminal-justice, sentencing, or policing measures are included.
The bill has no trade, tariff, or globalization provisions.
By authorizing new discretionary spending without offsetting cuts or revenue, the bill accepts additional deficit financing.
No provisions address LGBTQ+ legal protections or rights.
Foreign aid is not mentioned.
The legislation contains no voting or election-related content.
Section 3(f) requires de-identification, HIPAA compliance, and privacy protections for maternal-health data, modestly strengthening data-protection rules.
No labor, union, or workplace-flexibility provisions appear.
The bill does not address religious exemptions or conflicts with anti-discrimination rules.
